lesson.title: IP Addresses: Giving Every Interface a Findable Place
lesson.summary: Explains the IP address as the hierarchical, logical address assigned to a network interface that enables routing across the wider internet, contrasting it with the flat, hardware based MAC address.
lesson.body:
While a MAC address identifies a network interface for delivery within a single local network segment, reaching across the wider internet requires a different kind of address, one that reflects where an interface sits within the network's overall structure rather than just which specific piece of hardware it is. That address is called an IP address, short for Internet Protocol address, and it is what routers throughout the network core use to decide, hop by hop, which direction to forward a packet in order to eventually reach its destination.

The most widely deployed version, IPv4, uses a 32-bit address, conventionally written as four numbers between 0 and 255 separated by periods, a format called dotted decimal notation, for example 203.0.113.5. Because the internet has grown to connect far more interfaces than IPv4's roughly four billion possible addresses can uniquely support, a newer version, IPv6, uses a much larger 128-bit address, written as eight groups of hexadecimal digits separated by colons, offering an enormously larger address space for the long term.

Unlike a MAC address, which is flat and tied permanently to a piece of hardware, an IP address is hierarchical and logical: it is assigned based on which network an interface is currently connected to, and it can change if the interface moves to a different network or is reassigned. This hierarchical structure is what lets routers in the network core forward traffic efficiently, groups of IP addresses can be aggregated and treated as a single group heading in the same general direction, the way postal codes let mail get sorted toward a region before being sorted down to a specific street. A router does not need to know the exact path to every single IP address in existence, only the right general direction to send a packet based on the address's structure.

Consider a worked example that draws together several earlier sections. Your laptop's WiFi network interface is assigned an IP address by your home router, commonly something in a private range like 192.168.1.10, when it joins your home network. That address is only meaningful within your home network. Your home router itself has a different, public IP address, assigned by your internet service provider, that other networks across the internet can actually route toward. When your laptop sends a request to a web server, that server's own interface has its own IP address, for instance 203.0.113.5, and it is that address, examined by every router in the network core, that guides your packet across the mesh of the internet, hop by hop, until it arrives at the correct network, and finally the correct interface.

Because IP addresses are assigned per interface, exactly like MAC addresses, a host with multiple interfaces, discussed two sections ago, will have a separate IP address for each one that is active, one for its WiFi interface and a different one for its Ethernet interface, should both be connected at the same time. This interface level precision is what finally sets up the last concept in this chapter: even once a packet has reached the right interface using its IP address, a host is often running many different applications at once, and something more is needed to deliver data to the correct one, which is exactly the job of the port number.
